questions.q: Why is Supplier Import commonly one of the first FBDI loads run in a new Oracle Fusion implementation?
options: Because almost nothing else in Payables or Procurement can happen until suppliers exist in the system
Because suppliers are the least important data in the system
Because supplier data never needs validation
Because it is the only FBDI template Oracle provides
questions.explain: Payables invoices, purchase orders, and procurement activity all depend on supplier records already existing, which is why loading suppliers typically comes first.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does the Supplier Import template generate two separate CSV files?
options: Because the macro always produces exactly two files regardless of content
Because 25 rows is too many for a single file
Because one file is a backup copy of the other
Because the template has two data tabs — supplier and site — each mapping to its own interface table
questions.explain: Each data tab in a multi-tab template maps to a distinct interface table, so each tab generates its own CSV file.

questions.q: In the example, one of the 25 supplier rows is rejected for a duplicate supplier number. What does this tell you?
options: The ZIP file itself was corrupted
The business-rule validation during the supplier import process caught a supplier number that already exists in the system
The file was uploaded to the wrong account entirely
Macros were disabled in Excel
questions.explain: A duplicate-value rejection is a business-rule validation failure, caught during the product-specific import process — not a file-format or upload problem.

questions.q: Which UCM account should the supplier ZIP file be uploaded into?
options: Any account — the account chosen has no effect
The account scoped to general ledger journal imports
The account scoped to supplier/procurement imports
The account scoped to payables invoice imports
questions.explain: As covered in lesson 4, uploading to the wrong account leaves the file invisible to the process meant to find it. Supplier data needs the supplier/procurement import account.

questions.q: In the example, a rejected row had 'Corporate Supplier' typed into the supplier type field instead of the correct configured code. What kind of mistake is this?
options: Typing a lookup label instead of the exact coded value the field expects
A macro security setting blocking CSV generation
A UCM account mismatch
A ZIP file that failed to upload
questions.explain: This is the classic lookup-code mistake from lesson 6 — the system needs the exact configured code, not a human-friendly label, even if the label is understandable.
